nameStory: The "three-parted" name comes from this plant's distinctive leaves, which are divided into three main sections or lobes. The "beggarticks" part of the name refers to the sneaky way this plant's seeds stick to your clothes and pet fur with tiny barbed hooks, like a persistent beggar who won't let go!
description: Three-parted Beggarticks is a weedy annual herb that grows 1-4 feet tall in wet areas throughout New England. It produces small, inconspicuous yellow flower heads that lack the showy petals you'd expect from a sunflower family member. The plant is most noticeable in late summer and fall when its sticky, barbed seeds latch onto anything that brushes past. Despite being in the same family as daisies and sunflowers, this humble plant focuses more on seed dispersal than flashy flowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are divided into three distinct, toothed sections (tripartite), giving them a hand-like appearance. The leaf segments feel somewhat rough and papery when rubbed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, yellow flower heads lack the white petals of typical daisies - just tiny yellow disk flowers clustered together. The flowers have a faint, earthy smell and are surrounded by leafy green bracts.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, brown seeds with 2-4 barbed bristles that feel like tiny fishhooks when you try to remove them from clothing. They make a soft rattling sound when shaken in a closed hand.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a branching annual herb, often forming small colonies in muddy areas. Stems are typically smooth and somewhat succulent-feeling when squeezed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves attach directly opposite each other on the stem (not alternating), and the three-part division extends nearly to the base of each leaf.

habitat: Look for Three-parted Beggarticks in wet, muddy areas like pond edges, stream banks, ditches, and seasonal wetlands throughout New England. It thrives in disturbed, nutrient-rich soils and often grows alongside other moisture-loving plants like jewelweed and various sedges. You'll commonly find it in areas that flood seasonally but may dry out partially in late summer.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms, producing small seedlings with the characteristic three-part leaves in muddy areas.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly through summer, developing their branching structure and beginning to flower by mid to late summer with small yellow blooms.
seasonality.fall: Peak identification time as plants produce abundant sticky seeds that readily attach to clothing and animal fur. Seeds remain viable and clingy well into fall.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, but seeds remain in the soil and on surrounding vegetation, waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Three-parted Beggarticks seeds are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired the invention of Velcro - the tiny hooks on each seed work exactly like the hook side of this famous fastener, grabbing onto any loop-like surface they encounter!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other beggarticks species, but the three-parted leaves are distinctive - most other beggarticks have simple, undivided leaves or leaves divided into five or more parts. Memory trick: "Three-parted = three parts" - count the leaf divisions!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its weedy reputation and humble appearance, Three-parted Beggarticks is actually a native plant in much of its range and provides late-season nectar for small bees and flies when few other flowers are available.
compareHints: Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage. The leaf shape alone usually distinguishes it from its relatives, making it one of the easier beggarticks to identify.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
